paragraphs.heading: A star still being born
paragraphs.text: A protostar is a star in its infancy, still pulling in material from the molecular cloud it was born in. It marks the very first stage in a star's life story. For a star with the Sun's mass or less, this stage lasts around 500,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: How the collapse starts
paragraphs.text: Stars begin in small, dense patches of molecular cloud called dense cores. At first each core holds steady: its own gravity squeezes it inward, while gas pressure and magnetic pressure push it outward. As the core gathers more mass from the bigger cloud around it, gravity wins and the core starts to fall in on itself. The protostar stage begins when a fragment collapses like this and an opaque core, held up by its own pressure, forms inside it.

paragraphs.heading: A disk around the newborn
paragraphs.text: Gas falling toward the center first builds a small protostar, and then a disk that orbits it, called a protoplanetary disk. As the collapse goes on, more and more of the gas lands on the disk instead of the star, a result of angular momentum conservation. How material in the disk then spirals in onto the protostar is still not understood. Its outer surface is made at least partly of shocked gas that has dropped from the inner edge of the disk, so it looks very different from the calmer surface of a more settled star.

paragraphs.heading: Where its energy comes from
paragraphs.text: Ordinary stars make their energy by nuclear fusion in their centers. A protostar is cooler deep inside, and at its center ordinary hydrogen, hydrogen-1, is not yet fusing with itself. Its energy instead comes from radiation released at shock fronts, both on the star's own surface and on the face of its disk. Theory does predict one reaction: the hydrogen isotope deuterium, or hydrogen-2, fuses with hydrogen-1 to make helium-3, and that heat tends to puff the protostar up.

paragraphs.heading: Hidden behind dust
paragraphs.text: Light from the protostar has to pass through the dust of the dense core around it. The dust soaks up every photon that reaches it and sends the energy back out at longer wavelengths. So a protostar cannot be seen in visible light, and it cannot be placed on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram the way older pre-main-sequence stars can. Its glow is predicted to come out in the infrared and millimeter ranges.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting candidates
paragraphs.text: Point-like sources of this long-wavelength light are often seen in regions hidden behind molecular clouds. Those labeled Class 0 or Class I are widely thought to be protostars. Even so, there is still no firm proof that this is what they are.

paragraphs.heading: How the stage ends
paragraphs.text: The protostar stage ends once the infalling gas runs out. What is left is a pre-main-sequence star, which keeps shrinking until hydrogen starts fusing into helium and it becomes a main-sequence star. This picture was first put forward by Chushiro Hayashi in 1966. The earliest models made protostars far too big; later calculations, backed by observations, showed they are only a little bigger than main-sequence stars that have the same mass.
